title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
extended_summary:
This paper examines how an AI-assisted lesson planning system, Shiksha Copilot, was used to support teachers in low-resource public schools. The central problem is that teachers in such settings face heavy administrative burdens, limited instructional resources, and substantial time constraints, making it difficult to create high-quality lesson plans that are both pedagogically sound and aligned with mandated curricula. The authors ask how teachers collaborate with generative AI in lesson planning, what implementation challenges arise in multilingual classrooms, and how an LLM-based tool reshapes teachers’ work practices.

Shiksha Copilot was deployed in government schools across Karnataka, India, supporting English- and Kannada-medium lesson planning for Grades 5–10. The system used retrieval-augmented generation to draft curriculum-aligned lesson plans, a human-in-the-loop curation workflow in which expert curators reviewed and edited AI-generated lesson objectives and plans, and a translation module for Kannada. Teachers then accessed curated lesson plans through a distribution platform and customized them for their classrooms. A subset of teachers also received access to additional AI tools such as lesson-specific chat, general educational chat, and question generation. The study combined system logs, interviews, and pre/post surveys from 1,043 teachers and 23 curators, making it a large mixed-methods deployment study.

The findings suggest that the system was useful both for instructional planning and for bureaucratic documentation. English lesson plans were generally rated as high quality with relatively few edits, while Kannada translations required much more extensive linguistic correction. Teachers often made few recorded edits, but interviews showed they routinely adapted plans off-platform using their own expertise, peer networks, and classroom knowledge. Overall, the paper concludes that teacher-AI collaboration can reduce workload, lower stress, and support more activity-based pedagogy, but that meaningful change in low-resource settings depends on strong human oversight, localization, and attention to organizational constraints. The authors argue for human-in-the-loop, community-driven approaches to generative AI in education, especially for multilingual contexts in the Global South.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods field deployment with surveys, logs, and interviews, but it is not a randomized or quasi-experimental causal design. The study is strong descriptively, yet credibility for causal claims is limited by self-selection, no control group, and mostly qualitative/observational evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful workload relief and workflow integration, but the text provided does not give a quantitative effect size for the main benefits. Overall impact appears modest-to-clear for teachers in a priority population, but not large enough to justify a higher tier from the evidence shown.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-facing generative AI system for curriculum-aligned lesson-plan generation, curation, translation, and lesson-specific Q&A support in low-resource Kannada- and English-medium government schools.

Human-in-the-loop AI curation and validation of generated lesson plans, including review of learning objectives, content blocks, translations, and assessment items for pedagogical quality, accuracy, and contextual relevance.

finding.finding_summary: Shiksha Copilot reduced lesson-planning and record-keeping burden for teachers. The paper reports measurable reductions in lesson planning time and teacher stress, with teachers using the system both for classroom instruction and bureaucratic documentation; however, the excerpt does not provide a numeric effect size in the text shown. Teachers also used the system to generate plans in one sitting, indicating time-saving utility in a high-workload setting.
finding.measure: Survey measures of weekly time spent on lesson planning and administrative tasks; teacher stress scale (TSS); system logs and interviews on workflow use
finding.study_size: n=406 survey matched responses; n=22 teacher interviews; 1,043 total teachers deployed

finding.finding_summary: The tool supported administrative documentation and fit existing school workflows, but broader pedagogical change was constrained by staffing shortages and administrative demands. The paper describes organizational change in lesson-planning practices and workflow integration across 757 schools in 35 districts, but the impact on deeper instructional transformation was limited by institutional constraints.
finding.measure: Interview themes and deployment analysis of workflow change; descriptive use across schools/districts
